meta.methodology: Human-curated briefs reviewed against linked primary sources. These records are merged with, but not overwritten by, the automated policy-brief pipeline.

briefs.title: New person-based measure estimates 53% of U.S. adults own their home
briefs.summary: The Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis proposes the Homeowners-to-Population Ratio (HPOP), a person-based complement to the household-based owner-occupancy rate. Using American Community Survey microdata, HPOP classifies adult reference persons and their spouses or unmarried partners in owner-occupied homes as homeowners. For 2024, the researchers estimate that 53% of U.S. adults were homeowners, compared with an owner-occupancy rate of roughly 65%. HPOP sits about 12 points below the roughly 65% household-based owner-occupancy rate — the gap reflecting adults who live in owner-occupied homes without being the owner or their spouse/partner (e.g., adult children or other relatives). Among adults under 35, HPOP was about 22% — well below the roughly 37% owner-occupancy rate for households headed by someone under 35, which is a household-based measure and therefore not directly comparable. For Colorado, 2024 HPOP was 57.2% versus a 66.0% owner-occupancy rate — above the national HPOP. Because HPOP is published only at the state and metro (CBSA) levels, the available Colorado geographies are the state plus four metros: Fort Collins (HPOP 68.9%), Colorado Springs (68.5%), Denver-Aurora-Lakewood (63.2%), and Pueblo (41.5%). HPOP is not published for counties or places, so it cannot be reported for smaller Colorado jurisdictions such as Ignacio or Fruita. Source: Minneapolis Fed HPOP data, 2024.
briefs.implications: For COHO, HPOP should complement—not replace—the owner-occupancy rate. It can add person-level context to developer-oriented ownership analysis, including co-resident adults, delayed household formation, and disparities by age and demographic group. HPOP does not verify deed title for every adult, prove that co-resident adults will form separate households, or guarantee future rental demand. Local application should pair available state or metro HPOP estimates with household formation, cost burden, income, tenure, and supply data.

briefs.title: Colorado fee reductions for affordable housing: what towns waive, who pays, and how it differs by region
briefs.summary: COHO read the codes, fee schedules and council records of 46 Colorado jurisdictions and verified 115 local fee measures and 63 land-use or zoning incentives that lower the cost of affordable housing. Most fee relief is discretionary — 65 of 102 one-time fee measures need council or staff approval — and 93 of 115 fee measures do not say how the waived money is replaced. State law lets a local government waive an impact fee for low- or moderate-income or affordable employee housing (C.R.S. 29-20-104.5(5)) but does not require it, and a water or sewer utility run as an enterprise must keep grants from state and local governments under 10% of its annual revenue to stay outside TABOR. Consistent with that, utility fees are the ones cities repay from another fund: Loveland's Community Housing Development Fund repaid up to $366,070 of waived utility fees for Mirasol Phase III, while up to $504,807 of capital expansion fees on the same project were waived with no repayment, and Longmont may subsidize water and sewer system development fees only with money appropriated outside its utility funds. The regions differ. Mountain resort towns mostly waive fees outright for deed-restricted homes without an income cap — Mountain Village charges $21,650 per tap for a deed-restricted employee condo against $43,300 for a single-family home, and Telluride waives the in-town water and sewer tap attributable to a deed-restricted unit. Western Slope programs scale by income: Grand Junction waives 100% of city impact fees for rentals at or below 70% AMI, 75% at 71–80% AMI and 50% at 81–90% AMI, for a 30-year commitment. Front Range cities lean toward partial reductions, rebates after payment and income-qualified utility bill help: Colorado Springs rebates up to 100% of development charges after they are paid, Fort Collins credits up to $14,000 per unit, Littleton rebates $2,500 per affordable unit, Denver cuts the building permit fee $6,500 per income-restricted unit, and Westminster credits income-qualified households $360 a year on water bills. Deferrals (Fort Collins, Lafayette, Salida, Avon) are listed separately because a deferred fee is still owed. Screening context, not a study: what a jurisdiction offers is not what a project will receive.
briefs.implications: Four practical points. First, check who charges each fee: a town waiver may not reach a separate district — Aspen cannot waive school or sanitation district fees, and Grand Junction's program covers only city water and sewer, not Ute Water or Clifton Water. A special district has its own power to waive, amortize or defer its taps for affordable housing (C.R.S. 32-1-1001(1)(j)(II)), so the district is a separate ask. Second, count a waiver only once it is committed to the project; most are discretionary and several are subject to annual appropriation. Third, model a deferral as a loan with its trigger, not as a cost cut. Fourth, ask how a waiver is paid for: programs that name the paying fund (Grand Junction, Brighton, Loveland, Longmont) show where the money comes from; most do not. On land use, the 63 verified incentives in 37 jurisdictions are mostly inclusionary zoning with offsets, 90-day expedited review tied to the Proposition 123 fast-track, density bonuses and parking reductions. The Proposition 123 fast-track is a review deadline, not a fee rule. No Colorado statute found requires a local fee waiver for affordable housing; state bills since 2021 list fee waivers only as one optional strategy (HB21-1117, HB21-1271, HB24-1152, HB24-1313, SB24-174). Each jurisdiction's verified measures appear in its Housing Needs Assessment under local resources. The legal basis, how waived fees are paid for, the trends and numbered sources are in docs/methodology/LOCAL-JURISDICTION-HOUSING-CONTRIBUTIONS.md; the data is data/policy/fee-reductions.json.

briefs.title: HB26-1065 and Colorado’s Transit Zone credit: what the law establishes, what the draft QAP proposes, and what remains unknown
briefs.summary: Colorado HB26-1065 became law on May 27, 2026 and created Transit and Housing Investment Zones (THIZ), a state affordable-housing income-tax credit, and a separate sales-tax-increment mechanism for qualifying transit investment projects. The housing credit may be allocated by CHFA from 2027 through 2033, up to $8,333,333 annually, and is claimed over six credit years. Geographic eligibility depends on the official OEDIT THIZ map: the statute uses a two-mile zone around transportation facilities identified on that map. COHO’s tracked source was last checked September 26, 2026 and still recorded the map as not published, with publication due October 30, 2026. Transit-stop proximity therefore remains a screen, not an eligibility determination. CHFA’s 2027–2028 QAP Third Draft calls the housing credit the Transit Zone (TZ) credit. The draft says it may be awarded under a separate TZ Credit Allocation Plan in lieu of standard state credit, not in addition to it. Under the draft maximum-credit schedule, a 9% award may pair with a fixed $650,000 annual state or TZ credit in 2027 and $675,000 in 2028; a Round Two 4% award may pair with up to $675,000 annually in 2027 and $600,000 in 2028. Alternative amounts apply if the proposed state gap-funding pilot is unavailable. These are annual credit amounts, not total project proceeds, and the QAP terms are not final until adopted.
briefs.implications: The law, the OEDIT map and the QAP answer different questions. HB26-1065 creates the programs and statutory limits. OEDIT’s map determines whether an exact site is inside an eligible THIZ. CHFA’s QAP and separate allocation plan govern how an eligible rental project competes for and pairs the TZ credit. The draft QAP’s ordinary TOD/TOC location criterion is separate: it proposes five points for a qualifying site within a half-mile walk of transit, but those points do not themselves establish THIZ eligibility and are not TZ-credit-specific. The enacted bill and fiscal note do not create a distinct rural credit set-aside, bonus or enhanced rural amount; statewide geographic equity is a consideration for transit investment projects, not a substitute for zone eligibility. Until OEDIT publishes the authoritative map and CHFA adopts final rules, a project should record the exact site, retain the screen as preliminary, show TZ funding as unavailable rather than zero, and avoid adding draft credit proceeds to a development budget. The Deal Calculator reads the same canonical legislation record and displays the applicable 9% or 4% draft pairing only after supported map eligibility; it does not silently add the amount to the capital stack.

briefs.title: The permanent 12% increase in the 9% LIHTC state ceiling: what the 2025 federal law changed
briefs.summary: Public Law 119-21 (H.R. 1), approved on July 4, 2025, changed how much housing credit each state may award every year. Section 70422(a) of the law amends section 42(h)(3)(I) of the Internal Revenue Code. Each state has an annual housing credit ceiling: the authority its housing credit agency uses to award credits outside the tax-exempt bond route, mainly the competitive credits commonly called 9% credits. Part of that ceiling is the greater of a per-resident amount or a small-state minimum. For calendar years beginning after December 31, 2025, the amended law multiplies both of those amounts by 1.12, a 12% increase, after the annual cost-of-living adjustment. The amended provision sets no end year. The same provision previously gave a 12.5% increase for 2018 through 2021 only. For 2026, IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-32 sets the amount at the greater of $3.416 per resident or $3,953,600, and lists the section 70422(a) amendment among the changes it reflects.
briefs.implications: The increase applies only to the per-resident or minimum amount. The other parts of a state's ceiling, which are unused credit carried forward from the prior year, credit returned during the year, and any national-pool allocation, are not multiplied. Section 70422(a) changes the size of each state's annual credit authority; it does not change the credit rate, the income and rent tests, or the eligible-basis rules for an individual building. The law's only other change to section 42 is the tax-exempt bond-financing test in section 70422(b), which COHO tracks as a separate record. In Colorado, CHFA allocates federal housing credits and administers the program under its Qualified Allocation Plan. Colorado's total for a year depends on the state population figure used and on any carried-forward or returned credit. COHO has not verified a 2026 Colorado total published by CHFA, so this brief does not state one. The legislation record lists January 1, 2026 as the effective date of the change.

briefs.title: The 25% bond-financing test for 4% LIHTC buildings: what the 2025 federal law changed
briefs.summary: Public Law 119-21 (H.R. 1), approved on July 4, 2025, changed the tax-exempt bond test that lets a building claim housing credits without an allocation from the state's annual credit ceiling. Buildings that qualify this way receive the credits commonly called 4% credits. Section 70422(b) of the law rewrites section 42(h)(4)(B) of the Internal Revenue Code. Before the change, the test had one route: tax-exempt private activity bonds counted against the state's volume cap had to finance 50% or more of the aggregate basis of the building and the land under it. The amended provision keeps that 50% route and adds a second one. A building also qualifies if such bonds finance 25% or more of that basis, as long as one or more of those bonds come from an issue dated after December 31, 2025 and together finance at least 5% of the basis. The change applies to buildings placed in service in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025. The amended provision sets no end year.
briefs.implications: A building can now meet the test with a smaller share of bond financing than before, so the same amount of volume cap can support credits for more buildings. Bonds issued before 2026 still count toward the 25%, but only when bonds from post-2025 issues together provide at least 5% of the basis; that 5% can come from more than one such bond. For a rehabilitation that is treated as a separate new building, section 70422(b)(2)(B) treats both the existing building and the rehabilitation as placed in service on the date the rehabilitation expenditures are. The change does not alter the credit rate, the income and rent tests, or the state's annual credit ceiling. The law's other change to section 42, the 12% ceiling increase in section 70422(a), has its own COHO brief. In Colorado, the Department of Local Affairs receives the state's volume cap; CHFA's December 4, 2025 stakeholder presentation says that by statute 50% goes to statewide authorities, including CHFA, and 50% to local governments. In the same presentation CHFA said new CHFA multifamily lending and 2026 Round Two projects would use not more than 45% bond financing, lower when feasible. COHO has not verified a CHFA policy for later years, so this brief does not state one.

briefs.title: The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act: what the 2026 federal housing law changes for affordable rental financing
briefs.summary: H.R. 6644, the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, became law on July 11, 2026 as Public Law 119-101. A note by the Office of the Federal Register on the law says it was presented to the President on June 29, 2026 and became law without his signature because it was not returned within the time the Constitution allows. The House gave its final approval on June 23, 2026. The law reforms federal housing-supply and HUD programs. It does not amend section 42 of the Internal Revenue Code, so it does not change housing tax credit ceilings, credit rates or eligibility rules. Section 1202 says no additional funds are authorized to be appropriated to carry out the law or its amendments.
briefs.implications: The provisions below bear most directly on financing affordable rental housing. Section 204 makes the new construction of affordable housing an eligible Community Development Block Grant activity, limited to 20% of the amounts allocated to the recipient, and only for amounts appropriated after the date of enactment. Section 501 changes the HOME Investment Partnerships program: section 501(i) repeals the rule under which a participating jurisdiction lost the right to draw HOME funds it had not committed within 24 months, and section 501(l) exempts four categories of HOME activity from review under the National Environmental Policy Act: new construction infill housing projects, acquisition of real property for affordable housing, certain rehabilitation projects, and new construction projects of 15 units or less. An infill housing project must, among other tests, sit on previously disturbed land of not more than 5 acres. HUD must issue any rules it determines necessary for the exemptions within 1 year of enactment. Section 405(a) lets a voucher unit in a housing tax credit building meet the Housing Choice Voucher inspection requirement if it was physically inspected and met the suitability-for-occupancy requirement in section 42(i)(3)(B)(ii) during the preceding 12 months, and the public housing agency performed that inspection itself or can obtain its results. COHO searched the Federal Register on October 11, 2026 and found no HUD rule or notice putting the section 204 or section 501 changes into effect, so this brief does not describe how HUD will apply them. COHO has not verified any Colorado grantee's plan to use the new CDBG activity.

briefs.title: Livability beyond the pro forma: universal and functional design, privacy, shared space and green infrastructure in affordable housing
briefs.takeaway: Design for everyone who will live in the building over its life: step-free, easy to understand, quiet, private and green. That is where the evidence for livability is strongest, CHFA already requires or scores part of it, and the rest costs least when it is settled before the first drawing.
briefs.summary: The qualities residents feel every day, such as whether they can get in the door, find their way, close a door for privacy, meet a neighbor or look at a tree, do not appear in a pro forma. The research on them is uneven. Evidence is strongest for green infrastructure: a randomized trial in Philadelphia found that greening vacant lots reduced shootings, and a second analysis of the same trial found that nearby residents reported feeling depressed less often. Following the same people over 17 years, a UK panel study found that people reported higher life satisfaction and less distress in the years they lived in greener urban areas. Evidence on universal design is mostly about need rather than outcomes: under 5% of U.S. homes are livable for someone with moderate mobility difficulties and under 1% are wheelchair accessible, while the people who will need those features are a large and growing share of residents over a building's life. Evidence on shared space and on privacy is real but mostly observational or qualitative. CHFA's 2027-28 QAP Third Draft already requires green building certification, water-wise landscaping and the same unit design for every income tier, and awards two points for universal design or accessible Type A units in at least 5% of units.
briefs.implications: Treat universal design as the organizing idea rather than an add-on: a building that a wheelchair user, a parent with a stroller, an older resident and a new arrival who does not read English can all use without help is also easier to lease, manage and keep occupied. Most of it is cheap only at the start. Step-free routes, door widths, blocking for grab bars and room sizes are set by the site plan and the first floor plans, and are expensive to change later. Green infrastructure in Colorado should mean shade trees, native and water-wise planting and usable outdoor rooms, because CHFA now limits non-functional turf. Smaller homes can live well when the plan does the work: storage where it is used, a real entry, rooms that fit furniture, one-floor living for older residents and a porch deep enough to sit on. Put shared rooms on the routes residents already walk, such as the entry, mailroom and laundry, rather than behind a locked door at the end of a corridor. Do not put a dollar value on any of this in a deal model. The studies do not support one, and a made-up number is worse than none. Use this brief to decide design priorities and to write the QAP narrative, and use the Deal Calculator for the numbers it can actually support.

sections.heading: Universal design: spaces anyone can use without help
paragraphs: Universal design means designing a place so that as many people as possible can use it, without adaptation and without being singled out. The seven principles written at North Carolina State University's Center for Universal Design in 1997 are still the clearest test: equitable use, flexibility in use, simple and intuitive use, perceptible information, tolerance for error, low physical effort, and size and space for approach and use. Four of the seven are about usability, not access codes. A space can pass an accessibility inspection and still be hard to use.

The need is large and mostly unmet. HUD's analysis of the 2011 American Housing Survey found that about a third of U.S. homes could be modified for a person with a mobility disability, under 5% were livable for someone with moderate mobility difficulties, and under 1% were wheelchair accessible. Smith, Rayer and Smith (2008) projected how aging will raise the number of households with a disabled member and concluded that a home built today will very likely house someone with a disability during its life. An affordable rental building will house many households over its compliance period and after it, so it should be designed for the residents it will have later as well as the first ones.

Federal rules set a floor, not a goal. The Fair Housing Act requires seven accessibility features in covered multifamily buildings first occupied after March 13, 1991: in every unit of an elevator building, and in ground-floor units otherwise. Projects with HUD funds, such as HOME, must also meet Section 504: at least 5% of units accessible for people with mobility impairments and another 2% for people with hearing or vision impairments. CHFA's draft QAP adds two points for universal design or for Type A accessible units in at least 5% of units. Zero-step entrances and wider doors cost little when planned into new construction and are much harder to add later (Maisel, Smith and Steinfeld, 2008).
sections.items_heading: What highly usable looks like in practice
items: One step-free route from the sidewalk, parking, drop-off and transit stop to every entrance, and on to the mailroom, laundry, trash room, community room and outdoor space.
Entrances people can find and use with full hands: covered, well lit, a power-operated or easy-to-open door, a place to set things down, and seating nearby.
Wayfinding that works without signs: daylight at the ends of corridors, a different color or material at each floor and door, no dead-end corridors, and signs that can be read from a seated height.
Controls anyone can work: lever handles, rocker switches, thermostats and outlets within reach, front-control ranges and side-opening ovens, and enough clear floor space at the sink and the bed.
Bathrooms that adapt: curbless or low-threshold showers, wall blocking for grab bars in every unit, and room to turn around.
Benches with backs and arms, shade and glare-free lighting along walking paths, because people who cannot walk far without resting stop going out when there is nowhere to sit.
Rooms that flex as a household changes: a bedroom that can serve as an office or a carer's room, and a door that closes on the space where a child does homework.
sections.note: These practices follow the seven principles and the Fair Housing Act requirements. They were not each tested in a trial, and the brief does not claim they were.

sections.heading: Functional design: smaller homes that live well, and a porch that works
paragraphs: Affordable homes are often smaller than market-rate ones, and Colorado sets no floor. CHFA's QAP has no minimum unit size by bedroom count, while North Carolina's 2026 QAP requires at least 660 square feet for a one-bedroom and England's national space standard sets 50 square meters (about 540 square feet) for a one-bedroom home for two people, with 1.5 square meters of built-in storage. Size matters, but it is not the whole story. In a survey of 8,177 Milan students during the 2020 lockdown, living in an apartment under 60 square meters (about 650 square feet) raised the odds of moderate to severe depressive symptoms by about a third (odds ratio 1.31), and a poor view from the home raised them about as much (1.37).

Layout can make a small home feel bigger. In a study of 9-year-olds, Evans and Rollings found that higher bedroom ceilings weakened the link between feeling crowded at home and physiological stress. RIBA's survey of new English homes found the average three-bedroom home was about one single bedroom short of the London standard, which RIBA described as the space for a bed, bedside table, wardrobe, desk and chair. Testing a plan with real furniture is the simplest way to catch that. For older residents, one-floor living matters most: in a national sample of 7,197 adults aged 65 and older, having the kitchen, bedroom and bathroom on one floor was among the home features most strongly linked to staying in place rather than moving (Granbom et al., 2018).

The front porch is where privacy and community meet. Jan Gehl's studies of residential streets in Australia, Canada and Scandinavia found more lingering and street life where front yards, forecourts and porches form a 'soft edge' between home and street. In 10 Portland neighborhoods, Wilkerson and colleagues found more neighborliness where front porches and continuous sidewalks give people semi-private space for casual contact, though several of their results were not statistically significant. A porch only does this if it is usable. The London Plan sets 1.5 meters (about 5 feet) as the minimum depth and width for private outdoor space, which is roughly what a chair and a person need. A narrow stoop is only a step up to the door.
sections.items_heading: What makes a small home and its porch functional
items: Storage inside the home where it is used: an entry closet, a pantry, linen storage and bedroom closets, counted in the plan rather than left to leftover corners.
A defined entry: a place to stop, drop keys and bags, and take off boots, so the living room is not also the hallway.
A kitchen with a work surface that doubles as a table, such as an island or peninsula, when there is no room for a separate dining area.
Rooms checked against real furniture for the household the unit is meant for: beds, a dresser, a desk or homework table, and a table that seats everyone.
Daylight and a view from the main living space, and from two sides where the plan allows. Ceiling height is a cheap way to make a small room feel larger.
For older residents and anyone with limited mobility: the kitchen, a bedroom and a full bathroom on the entry level, with a step-free route from parking to the door.
A porch at least 5 feet deep, covered and lit, facing the shared walk rather than the parking lot, with room for two chairs and a privacy screen between neighbors.
A second, private outdoor space at the back, such as a patio or small yard, so the front porch can be social while the household still has somewhere private.
sections.note: The design items are practices consistent with the cited studies and standards. Apart from the cited findings, they have not each been tested in a trial.

sections.heading: From practice: questions from Fruita Mews, and what the research says
paragraphs: Fruita Mews Phase I is a 50-unit affordable townhome community in Fruita, with an individual porch for every home along tree-lined pedestrian walks. Phase II is a proposal that has applied to CHFA for housing tax credits. It has not been awarded, and its design may change.

In a March 2026 response to CHFA's questions on the Phase II application, the developer described what residents of Phase I valued and what went unused. Those are one team's observations, not an evaluation. This brief uses them as questions and sets each one beside the research that supports it, qualifies it, or leaves it untested.

table.caption: Fruita Mews observations and the research on each
rows: Residents valued their own front porches, front and rear entries and defined outdoor space. The Phase II proposal adds privacy screens on the porches.

Supported in part. Gehl's street studies and Wilkerson's Portland study link porches and front yards to more lingering and neighbor contact, though several of Wilkerson's results were not significant. The London Plan treats 1.5 meters (about 5 feet) as the minimum usable depth. No study found tested privacy screens on porches.
Detached exterior storage went largely unused. Residents preferred storage inside their homes, and the Phase II proposal moves that budget indoors.

Consistent, but untested directly. England's space standard requires built-in storage inside each home (1.5 square meters for a one-bedroom home for two people), and RIBA framed the space shortfall in new homes in terms of furniture and storage. No study found compared detached and in-unit storage use.
Older adults filled more of the one-bedroom homes than expected. The Phase II proposal groups single-story one-bedroom homes around a garden, next to family townhomes.

Supported. Having the kitchen, bedroom and bathroom on one floor was among the home features most linked to older adults staying in place (Granbom et al., 2018). Under 5% of U.S. homes suit someone with moderate mobility difficulties. Shared outdoor space and nearby greenery are linked to neighbor ties and higher well-being, though the shared-space evidence is mostly qualitative.
The Phase II plans add kitchen islands, defined entries, larger living areas and walk-in closets, and move entries off the face of the porch.

Partly supported. Layout and room volume can offset crowding stress (Evans and Rollings), and small size and poor views each raised the odds of depressive symptoms in the Milan lockdown study. Universal design's 'size and space for approach and use' supports clear entries. No study found tested kitchen islands or foyers on their own.

sections.note: Source for the left column: the developer's clarification response to CHFA on the Fruita Mews II application (March 2026), provided to COHO. Where a row says no study was found, that is a gap in the evidence, not evidence against the design.

sections.heading: Green infrastructure, health and happiness
paragraphs: This is the strongest body of evidence in the brief, and it includes randomized trials. The effects are small for any one person, but they apply to everyone living there and add up across a building.

In Colorado, green infrastructure should mean shade trees, native and water-wise planting, and outdoor rooms people use, not lawn. CHFA now limits non-functional turf. Shade matters here too: across 108 U.S. urban areas, formerly redlined neighborhoods are hotter at ground level than their neighbors, by as much as 7°C (about 12°F), and Denver had one of the largest gaps.

table.caption: What the studies found
rows: People in Philadelphia living near vacant lots that were greened reported feeling depressed and worthless less often; neighbors of untreated lots did not (South et al., 2018).
Greening vacant lots reduced shootings by 6.8% in the same Philadelphia trial (Branas et al., 2018).

The same people reported higher life satisfaction and less mental distress in the years they lived in greener urban areas. The effect was about a third of the life-satisfaction gain associated with marriage (White et al., 2013).
UK panel, 1991-2008, comparing the same people over time
Across more than a million smartphone mood reports, people were happier outdoors in natural settings than in built-up ones (MacKerron and Mourato, 2013).
People who spent at least 120 minutes a week in nature were more likely to report high well-being and good health; under 120 minutes showed no benefit (White et al., 2019).
Danish children with the least green space near home had up to 55% higher risk of later psychiatric disorders than those with the most (Engemann et al., 2019).
Chicago public housing residents assigned to buildings with more trees and grass outside reported less aggression and violence (Kuo and Sullivan, 2001).

One year after a green rehab to Enterprise Green Communities standards, adults in a 60-unit Minnesota property reported better general health and less asthma, bronchitis and sinusitis (Breysse et al., 2011).
Before and after, no control group
Children with asthma in green public housing in Boston had fewer symptoms, attacks and asthma-related school absences than children in conventional units (Colton et al., 2015).

sections.heading: Shared space that people actually use
paragraphs: Shared space helps residents get to know neighbors, and that reduces loneliness, but most of the evidence is interviews and surveys rather than trials. Social-housing tenants in New Zealand, most of them over 55 and living alone, described common areas as where neighbor ties began and grew into mutual help. A survey of multifamily residents found that those with more shared amenities knew more neighbors and felt less lonely, and that everyday spaces such as lobbies and laundry rooms mattered as much as courtyards.

The size of the room matters less than where it is and what happens in it. A community room on the way to the mailboxes gets used; one behind a locked door at the end of a corridor does not. Resident services are part of the same picture: industry studies of properties with on-site services report lower rent arrears and fewer eviction move-outs, though none of them is a controlled study.

sections.heading: Privacy, crowding and quiet
paragraphs: Crowding is linked to worse wellbeing in children, with more distress, more conflict with parents and more learned helplessness, regardless of household income, and Gary Evans's research found the effects were stronger in large multifamily buildings. The design response is bedroom counts that fit the households the market study expects, a door that closes on a place to study, and enough storage that a living room does not become a storeroom.

Quiet is privacy you can hear. The WHO's 2018 noise guidelines link traffic noise to disturbed sleep and cardiovascular disease, which matters for sites next to highways and rail lines. Evidence on noise from neighbors is thinner, but complaints about it are common. Separate units acoustically, and keep mechanical equipment, trash rooms and elevators away from bedroom walls.

sections.heading: Safety and dignity
paragraphs: Oscar Newman's defensible-space argument, that building form drove crime in public housing, is better known than it is supported. A federal review found that only limited reliable conclusions could be drawn from his studies, and his central comparison did not account for the different share of children in the two projects. Clear sightlines, entrances that face the street and good lighting are still sensible. The evidence just does not show they are enough on their own.

Dignity has a direct rule in Colorado. CHFA’s QAP requires every income tier to get units with the same amenities and square footage, asks the same of market-rate units to the extent possible, and spreads affordable units through each building and, where it can, each floor. A separate wing of smaller or plainer affordable units works against that rule.

sections.heading: Limits of this brief
paragraphs: Most studies here are observational, small, or both, and several come from one research group. Only the Philadelphia greening trial is randomized. None of the studies measured effects on operating costs in Colorado affordable housing, so the brief gives no dollar figures, and none should be added to a deal model on its strength. The QAP items come from a draft. COHO checks each quoted requirement against the machine-extracted text of the named CHFA document on every build, but the PDF is the authority.
